title: Fork front, candidate revision: stronger seats for the yaw motor's five M3 screws. Nothing real is changed yet.
rows: Arm's design load, worst screw (104°): layer tension, 0.5 / 1 mm reading
Same on a finer mesh, 0.5 mm reading: layer tension / shear / overall
Other four screws, lowest of any measure
Roll stop at 17 N.m, lowest screw: layer tension / shear, 0.5 mm reading
Screws over-tightened to about 4x snug, worst screw: shear
notes: WHAT CHANGES (all hidden once assembled, except the skirt):

1. Each of the five screw seats: a flat for a standard M3 washer on an 8.0 mm floor (was 6.5), with a rounded corner into the pocket wall;
      2.5 mm round at the two screws under the cheek. Screws: M3 x 14 with one washer each, SNUG ONLY (see the last table row).
2. Key access to the 104° screw: a round tunnel in place of the square-ended slot; its opening is inside the drum's envelope, as today.
3. The skirt is exactly 3.00 mm longer (your decision with the taller hub).
4. Fit, on the fork rear: the bearing's outer race becomes a hand-push fit with no play (sized on a test ring first). The fork's strength depends on it.

ONE FIGURE IS UNDER TARGET: on the finer mesh, shear under the rim of the 104° washer reads 0.94 on the 0.5 mm reading (1.56 on the 1 mm reading).
      It is where the washer's rim presses into the plastic (in compression). A thicker washer does not change it and a wider one does not fit beside the motor.
Figures: washers modelled as real steel parts, plastic read alone, nothing left out. * rigid-washer model. ** 0.49 / 0.89 in layer tension, rigid-washer model.
Not checked: a print; a real motor's five M3 threads; the bearing fit on a test ring.
